📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At Coachella, fringe is welcome. Infringement, not so much.

In a new 28-page lawsuit filed Tuesday and obtained by Rolling Stone, organizers of the annual music festival accuse Walmart of “willful and repeated acts of trademark infringement,” claiming the retail giant intentionally sold, or allowed others to sell, “directly competitive goods” bearing the Coachella name and its distinctive logos featuring a Ferris wheel and palm tree silhouettes. The organizers say the unauthorized merchandise was sold in recent years at Walmart stores in North Indio and La Quinta, near the festival grounds. They also accuse Walmart of using Coachella’s trademarks in signage and advertising to promote other products, including beverages, coolers, and folding chairs.

Sources indicate that the festival and its parent firm, Goldenvoice, argue in their upcoming filings in federal court in Los Angeles that they’re highly selective in granting sponsorships and licensing deals. The arrangements, they argue, command considerable value given the festival’s reach and visibility, and Walmart is unfairly exploiting their intellectual property without authorization or payment.

“Walmart has intentionally created a likelihood of confusion and false association between Walmart’s stores, website, and various goods it sells, on the one hand, and the festival and plaintiffs’ goods, on the other hand,” the lawsuit reads.

The plaintiffs say the allegedly infringing conduct “was so extensive and so prominent” that a local newspaper, The Desert Sun, posted several videos on Instagram showing tumblers, bottles, wine glasses, tank tops, and other merchandise bearing the Coachella trademarks along with a caption that read, “Who needs the merch tent [at Coachella] when you have the North Indio Walmart?”.

It has been revealed that the complaint includes photos of the allegedly infringing items for sale at Walmart stores. The festival’s organizers say they have repeatedly asked Walmart to remove the merchandise over the years, but that the retailer “typically stops for a time but then resumes its infringing conduct.” They say the “recalcitrant behavior” left them with no choice but to sue. Trending Stories Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Dead at 65 Duran Duran’s Andy Taylor Was the Wildest of the Wild Boys The Country Song About Losing Your Virginity That Became an Enduring Hit Thank You, Jensen Huang.

In a statement sent to Rolling Stone, a spokesperson for Walmart noted the tech giant hasn’t seen the lawsuit yet. “We will review the complaint and respond appropriately in court once we are served,” the spokesperson said in an email. A rep for Goldenvoice did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Sources indicate that coachella recently revealed that Dua Lipa, Tame Impala, and SZA will top the lineup when the festival returns to Indio, California, next year. The fest is set for April 9-11 and April 16-18, 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo revealed its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.00, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:.

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $20 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

In a recent development, kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original released all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $49.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails for $69.99 for a physical copy on Switch 2, but Nintendo is selling it for $49 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally debuted on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The firm offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $48.97 before Black Friday.

Recent findings suggest that nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Industry observers note that nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo notes that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in Upcoming York and San Francisco. Breaking: SSH is a GUI framework

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zydra

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "One thing about which fish know exactly nothing is water." — Marshall McLuhan.
  • SSH is a tool so ubiquitous that we've forgotten what it actually is: a multiplexed, encrypted byte stream accessible on a cross-platform rendering engine that ships on every laptop, server, and phone on earth.
  • Industry observers note that to see just how far you can push it, I've made a microVM with a desktop environment designed from the ground up to render natively over SSH.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"One thing about which fish know exactly nothing is water." — Marshall McLuhan.

SSH is a tool so ubiquitous that we've forgotten what it actually is: a multiplexed, encrypted byte stream accessible on a cross-platform rendering engine that ships on every laptop, server, and phone on earth. A number of terminal protocols have slowly added graphics, clipboard sharing (including images), notifications, mouse support, and more on top of SSH.

Industry observers note that to see just how far you can push it, I've made a microVM with a desktop environment designed from the ground up to render natively over SSH. You can try it right now (no sign-up):.

All terminal protocols work on data that can be passed through SSH, so typically, any terminal protocol will extend to SSH.

Perhaps the most ubiquitous upcoming terminal protocol is the Kitty Graphics Protocol, which superseded the older Sixel and iTerm2 graphics protocols. It allows for compression, client-side graphical state (via VRAM), and even animations entirely on the terminal.

Recent findings suggest that graphics alone don't make a complete GUI, though. SSH has protocols that cover all other angles:.

Sources indicate that notifications: OSC 99 "Rich Notifications" allow image, text, and body. OSC 777 (our first fallback) allows only text and body, and OSC 9 (our last fallback) allows only a title.

We end up using a similar fallback for many things.

A few tricks make compositing over SSH fast. Firstly, where possible, especially when streaming terminals, we simply stream them as text rather than unnecessarily streaming it via graphics. The compositor's UI framework itself cleverly overlays traditional text over carefully aligned graphics, saving bandwidth. In the case of zydra.sh, this allows us to efficiently stream the entire cloud computer's desktop UI over SSH.

Next, we optimize graphics by sending a sort of "grid" of pixels. Each cell has its own updates, where the previous frame is compared to the current frame to catch and send updates, avoiding having to constantly stream the full screen. Kitty also offers both RGB and RGBA, and so by removing transparency where it's not needed, we save another 25% in bandwidth. We also track ping and other factors to determine how well the client handles the stream: lowering the resolution in select cells, especially when scrolling, to relieve pressure. We also use Kitty's client-side state to hold graphics ahead-of-time before they're displayed on screen, as well as holding repeated UI components.

Not all terminals support all the latest terminal protocols, so the compositor must also fallback to older graphics protocols Sixel and iTerm2, and when necessary, fall back to pure textual streaming, using ASCII to replicate some UI. In the case of notifications and other protocols, multiple protocols similarly exist, which we also gracefully fallback to when needed.

Parsing terminal versions and querying capabilities allows us to get an idea of what the client supports. We also continually verify that features work as expected on the client as the session boots. The Kitty terminal itself I've found to have very reliable support for all graphics protocols zydra.sh relies on.

Industry observers note that VNC is limited to sending pictures of the screen and diffing frames to find what changed. With zydra.sh's approach, apps directly tell the compositor what changed, and terminal text is sent as text you can select and copy natively. The browser is a WebKit build that delivers frames to the compositor as DMA-BUFs without a readback, which can be driven agentically via Playwright.

While webapps have advantages, especially in client-side state, WASM, and WebGPU, they don't really capture the universality and ease-of-use of an SSH session. SSH keys double as authentication, and -A allows you to SSH into servers from within a remote microVM itself. Webapps also can't be accessed from a pure TTY.

SSH also has sshfs, so you can mount your VM's filesystem locally:.

Industry observers note that on Android, SSH is technically "available" through Termux, although it can be finicky. I've made a webapp version of the zydra.sh compositor that's more responsive and accessible in mobile for this use case.

SSH also still poses limits around audio (as agents are increasingly used with dictation), and despite how much the Kitty graphics protocol helps, it leaves a lot of optimization on the table due to a lack of stronger client-side state and streaming protocols.

My SSH-native compositing system and microVM desktop environment based on it are the backbone of my broader attempt to create an actually pleasant agent sandbox :). A cloud computer without cloud friction if you will. Another article which describes how I added a "timeline" feature to zydra.sh that allows you to rewind the VM as if watching a livestream is available here: Agents need an undo button. You can read more about me and my background on my portfolio, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up….

In a recent development, the Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a substantial upgrade last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

The Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Sources indicate that even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people latest to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

Sources indicate that the Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a significant revision over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”.

Recent findings suggest that with the new system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

It has been revealed that as I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

Industry observers note that the Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people upcoming to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

What do you think of the current Apple Watch lineup? Are you shopping for one this holiday season? Let us know down in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Giles’ musical beginnings with Giles, Giles, and Fripp, a trio he cofounded in 1967 in Bournemouth — where was he was born on March 1, 1942 — with his brother Peter and guitarist Robert Fripp, were inauspicious, at least by King Crimson standards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michael Giles, a drummer and singer who cofounded King Crimson, died Monday, according to King Crimson’s record label, DGM, which did not report a cause of death. Giles was 84.

Recent findings suggest that “Michael’s originality, musical curiosity and uncompromising commitment to creative freedom challenged conventions and inspired generations of musicians around the world,” Crimson’s label noted. “He leaves behind an extraordinary musical legacy, and his unique contribution to the evolution of progressive music will never be forgotten.”.

Giles’ musical beginnings with Giles, Giles, and Fripp, a trio he cofounded in 1967 in Bournemouth — where was he was born on March 1, 1942 — with his brother Peter and guitarist Robert Fripp, were inauspicious, at least by King Crimson standards. The band’s only album, 1968’s The Cheerful Insanity of Giles, Giles and Fripp, was all psychedelia: shimmering organ, pensive vocals, and relatively straightforward, march-like drumming that only occasionally hinted at jazziness. It’s straightforward pop rock, but you can also hear how it provided the framework for King Crimson’s outré, ponderous adventures a year later.

Sources indicate that when Peter quit to become a solicitor’s clerk in November 1968, Michael and Fripp wanted to continue making music, so they formed King Crimson with Greg Lake, who’d played bass with the Gods, and multi-instrumentalist Ian McDonald. The lineup included Peter Sinfield as lyricist and lighting director. Together, the conceived an album that would define the sound of prog rock in the early Seventies: In the Court of the Crimson King, which came out in 1969.

Sources indicate that the album’s seven-minute opening cut, “21st Century Schizoid Man,” was an FM radio hit in spite of its turn-on-a-dime rhythm changes and extended bass and sax duets. The stylistic shift allowed Giles to challenge himself to make his drum parts more musical, whether mirroring McDonald’s sax or rolling rhythms like waves in the main riff. “The Court of the Crimson King,” a 10-minute musical journey, took the streamlined rock sound of Giles, Giles, and Fripp and augmented it with flute, Mellotron, and choral-like harmonies. Giles’ drumming on the song is the musical equivalent to expressionism as he brings out his bandmates’ drama. He latter cited Elvin Jones, who’d played with John Coltrane, as an inspiration. Pete Townshend called the album “an uncanny masterpiece.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

The band made its live debut in April 1969 and that July played before 650,000 music fans at the Rolling Stones’ Hyde Park concert. But it wouldn’t last. While on tour in the U.S., Giles and McDonald split off from the band to form a duo, as Fripp assumed more control of Crimson. Their debut, McDonald and Giles, arrived in 1970 and continued Crimson’s sound. But when Crimson looked like it was falling apart, Fripp was able to convince Giles to return for “guest drumming” on King Crimson’s second album, In the Wake of Poseidon, which also came out in 1970. Other than the live album, Epitaph, which featured live recordings from 1969, Giles’ association with Crimson ended there, though in the early 2000s he participated in the 21st Century Schizoid Band, a collective of other former King Crimson members without Fripp. Trending Stories Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Dead at 65 Duran Duran’s Andy Taylor Was the Wildest of the Wild Boys The Country Song About Losing Your Virginity That Became an Enduring Hit Thank You, Jensen Huang.

After King Crimson, Giles recorded with Leo Sayer, Kevin Ayers, Roger Glover, Neil Sedaka, and Bryan Ferry, among others. He also worked with former Crimson bandmates Greg Lake and McDonald on their albums. And he formed his own Michael Giles Mad Band, which released albums in 2009 and 2011. In 2001, he released a solo album, Progress, that he’d recorded in 1978 and in 2026 a compilation, Shadows/Solo.

Recent findings suggest that in a 2019 interview with Rolling Stone, Giles reflected on the legacy of “21st Century Schizoid Man.” “I knew we were doing something different, if not unique, in bringing rock and jazz together,” he noted. “Maybe it was nearer to some of Frank Zappa’s music — I don’t know. But the combination of Greg’s voice, Pete Sinfield’s words, heavy rock and free jazz made it very special and different from what had gone before, and the music of ’69.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the past few years Australia’s Telstra has run a campaign of “Free calls to Santa” from the universal service obligation funded payphones across the country – It’s a really fun idea and we wanted to replicate it on our network on Norfolk Island where we run the mobile network, but the’s no payphones.*.

  • Those who have seen my office / shed / studio / the HackHouse, know that I may have one or two payphones… But this needed a payphone that could stand the elements and be modern ish.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the past few years Australia’s Telstra has run a campaign of “Free calls to Santa” from the universal service obligation funded payphones across the country – It’s a really fun idea and we wanted to replicate it on our network on Norfolk Island where we run the mobile network, but the’s no payphones.*.

* There is now a payphone – You probably already guessed this.

Those who have seen my office / shed / studio / the HackHouse, know that I may have one or two payphones… But this needed a payphone that could stand the elements and be modern ish.

The answer, is of course, to use the sexiest payphone of all time; the Nortel Millennium. Featuring VFD display, durable keypad, card service, coin service, no fancy metering line required.

Unfortunately Nortel’s bankruptcy in 2008 meant I couldn’t phone up an account manager, but with the hookup of some guy with a U-Haul van full of Millennium’s in the US and a bit of a road trip, Cody from our team managed to pickup some really clean GTE branded payphones for the job.

Then Cody flew to Sydney where we drove to the house of someone who was heading to Norfolk the next day to explain they’d need to leave all their baggage at home as all of their baggage allowance was to be taken up with the weight of a payphone – Thanks Paul.

Eventually with the Payphone on Norfolk, we needed to get it programmed; for that there’s Howard Harte’s great mm_manager, which, with the aid of a USB modem is able to program the phones.

Sidebar: I also got this working with a softmodem (A fork of D-Modem with some minor tweaks I’ve documented here), so we could do it via straight SIP without the USB modem required – but the USB modem was the easier path.

The Philtel blog post covers how to setup your Millennium if you’re looking to play along at home yourself.

I hit a bit of a stumbling block with mm_manager as the software assumed you were part of the North American Numbering Strategy (NANP) – as one of the literally dozens of people who live outside of America, having to put a 1 in front of the number wasn’t going to fly.

After some trial and error I sussed out what bits on the config files that get pushed to the phone controls this and submitted a PR to mm_manager which is now merged.

We’re also able to set the messaging that appears on the screen, which I’m very happy with the branding on.

We set it for free-on-net calls, so anyone can call any Norfone number without charge and the Payphone tag number.

In a recent development, once this would’ve been the hard part, I did some work a long time ago with IBM Watson and built some stuff to annoy voters via phone with automated phone calls and capture their human responses and sort them and play the appropriate response. But tech has come a long way since 2019, and this was the easy part of the project.

We setup the payphone to make HOHOHO (464646) a destination that did not require coins when we did the rating table setup when programming the phone.

I’ve got 4 pre-recorded “Norfolk Specific” greetings to buy us time to get everything setup in the background, once these greetings play (each ends asking the caller their name) then we feed into the OpenAI API.

Recent findings suggest that one of the members from our team attempted to ask Santa to write a Python script to iterate over a for loop, while another team member asked Santa for firearms. In both cases it did a good job of redirecting.

All the code for this is on Github.

According to recent reports, the phone came GTE branded, so we needed to redo the card with the branding on it that goes around the screen. Two screws and some wiggling later we pulled out the card, and then I badgered my partner into using their day off to design a fresh one, with a retro style I really like.

The install was beautifully completed by long-time-reader-of-the-blog Minas from Shield Electrical and Air.

He knocked up a housing to Shield it from the rain and elements and installed it outside the office entrance.

The last step of the puzzle was making the phone so it could be captured by cult game Payphone Tag – I reached out to Alex and gave him the info, and now it’s there in the map for anyone to capture.

So with this now in place, we’ve still got to give it some tinsel and Christmas cheer, and I’ll get some more pics of it in place.

We’re waiting for someone to claim it on Payphone tag, and we’ve shipped 3 of these to another even more remote Island I’ll hopefully be able to share more info on later.

If you’re ever on Norfolk, give it a call.

Recent findings suggest that electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”.

It has been revealed that claude Ship is a latest product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic claims. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”.

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

Recent findings suggest that you can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here.

#119947. Marginal Grains

Marginal Grains

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Asteriskmag

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to Sumerian myth, when the world was young, there was no farming, no cattle, and no weaving.
  • In a recent development, together, Ashnan and Lahar furnished the rest of the pantheon with bread, beer, milk, and hides.
  • Recent findings suggest that the ancient Sumerians recognized something still true today: The story of wheat is the story of people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to Sumerian myth, when the world was young, there was no farming, no cattle, and no weaving. The original gods were forced to live in poverty. To solve this problem they created Ashnan, the goddess of grain, and Lahar, the god of sheep, and sent them to humans to cultivate their gifts.

In a recent development, together, Ashnan and Lahar furnished the rest of the pantheon with bread, beer, milk, and hides. But the newly introduced gods quarreled about which was greater. Enki, the god of wisdom, judged Ashnan the superior, reasoning that without grain there would be no bread, no beer, and, by extension, no cities and no Sumer.

Recent findings suggest that the ancient Sumerians recognized something still true today: The story of wheat is the story of people. Human consumption of wheat is older than cities, older than writing, older than the wheel. In fact, some of the very earliest surviving examples of writing, which, like wheat, originate in the Middle East, aren’t epic poems or religious texts but administrative records of the storage and taxation of grain. Other staple crops dominated in other parts of the world (like rice in East Asia, and maize in the Americas), but it was wheat that fueled the Roman Empire and the Industrial Revolution. Wheat now provides one-fifth of the world’s calories. The fact that it does so is thanks to centuries of human ingenuity and scientific improvement.

Six thousand years ago, when the Sumerian civilization was beginning to emerge in what is now Iraq, human consumption of grain was already ancient history. Remains of domesticated wheat from around 10,000 years ago have been found in Anatolia. These leftovers were wild emmer and einkorn (two progenitors of wheat), which looked a lot like the other wild grasses growing around them: a tall stalk topped by a small seed head. They were variably distributed throughout the landscape, and their seeds ripened at different times, so collecting them would have been laborious. Nonetheless, the people of the ancient Levant found the effort worthwhile, as the seeds were calorie-dense and stored well.

In a recent development, by farming wheat, humans unintentionally made it worse but also improved it. Wild wheat had reproduced without human assistance for millions of years. Its seeds, the grains that we eat, are attached to the head of the plant by a thin stalk called a rachis. When the seeds are mature, the rachis shatters, dispersing the seeds on the ground.

This process is essential for wild wheat to reproduce. Human intervention removed this selection pressure, allowing plants that did not shatter to reproduce. Because nonshattering is a recessive trait, nonshattering plants cannot produce shattering offspring.1 As a result, nonshattering plants proliferated, supplanting their wild predecessors. This is how archaeologists observed that domestication was underway.2.

It has been revealed that neolithic farmers collected and planted seeds from the heads of plants that remained intact, whereas seeds that had already fallen to the ground were less likely to be harvested or planted. Stores of emmer and einkorn dated as early as 7600 B.C.E. show rough scars, not the smooth tears left by spontaneous shattering, indicating that the natural reproductive process had been interrupted by harvesters. Once the seed-shattering trait had disappeared, wheat was almost completely dependent on humans collecting and planting its seeds to reproduce. In perhaps a thousand years, millions of years of selection for seed shattering had been undone.

On the positive side, yields went up. Grains grew bigger thanks to human cultivation. Naturally, grain size varied, but larger grains were less likely to be blown away or slip out of harvesters’ baskets and were therefore overrepresented in the seeds saved and replanted. On top of that, humans tend to plant seeds deeper than they naturally scatter, and larger seeds are more likely to germinate at greater depths. These processes are thought to have increased grain size by a quarter over the first 500 to 1,000 years of cultivation. By this time, wheat could no longer thrive without help from humans. But the transition to agrarian, sedentary communities enabled by bigger harvests also marked the beginning of our dependence on farming.

The next important step came just as wheat was beginning to spread to surrounding regions, when it absorbed a whole newly introduced set of genes from another species.

One way plants differ from animals is that they can hybridize much more easily, sometimes even happily adding whole new genomes to their own. Long before domestication, emmer wheat had already done this: Wild emmer is a naturally occurring amalgam of a cousin of einkorn and another species known as goat grass (Aegilops speltoides). Emmer is therefore tetraploid, meaning it has four sets of chromosomes.

It has been revealed that emmer and einkorn wheat diffused throughout Anatolia to Cyprus and beyond as farmers migrated out of the Fertile Crescent. Around this time, emmer hybridized again, incorporating the genome of a second species of goat grass (Aegilops tauschii), bringing its chromosome set count to six. This hybridized wheat, which first appears in the archaeological record in northeastern Turkey around 6000 B.C.E., thrived because it had two valuable traits. First, it was free-threshing. Before this, farmers had to pound grains with a mortar and pestle to free them from their tough outer husks, adding a labor-intensive step to every harvest. Second, this new hybrid had higher gluten content, meaning it could form stronger doughs that hold gas, allowing bread to rise. Initially, this saved labor and enabled tastier food. It is now known as bread wheat, or common wheat, and makes up more than 95% of wheat produced today.

Over the next several millennia, cultivation of bread wheat (and agriculture, more or less) spread throughout Europe and Asia. If a plant failed to grow in its fresh soil or was killed by autumn frosts before reaching maturity, it would be superseded by its better-acclimated relatives. Over thousands of years, incremental changes resulted in countless subtly different local “landrace” populations. Wheat also evolved through further hybridization with closely related plants. This is how we got spelt, which combined the larger grains of bread wheat with the strong shells of emmer, protecting it against the wet and cold and allowing it to thrive further north.

Much of this adaptation was probably incidental, just as early selection for larger seeds and nonbrittle rachises had been. But even in ancient times, careful attention was paid to wheat husbandry and to which varieties thrived in which environments. In 50 B.C.E., the Roman writer Varro advised farmers that “on the threshing-floor the largest and best ears should be placed apart, to furnish the best seed.”3 Long before genetics, farmers understood that good seed begat good crops. This contributed to thousands of years of gradual improvement and specialization.

According to recent reports, the Romans may have been intentionally selecting the best plants, but modern scientific wheat breeding began in western Europe in the 19th century. This dramatically sped up yield improvements. A fortuitously large number of early English estate records have survived, meaning we have data for wheat yields starting from before 1275, at which time farmers were producing around 0.6 metric tons per hectare. This was actually worse than the (continental) Romans, who achieved yields up to 1.3 metric tons per hectare.4 Yields remained approximately flat before the 16th century, when they began increasing (and have not stopped).

From the early 1600s through to 1805, yields in Britain almost doubled, increasing from 0.74 in 1604 to 1.26 metric tons per hectare in 1805.5 Deliberate plant selection contributed to this improvement, but intensive selection — that is, aggressively multiplying the very best strains — didn’t really take off until the second half of the 18th century.

In a recent development, farmers had always wanted to find high-performing seeds, but now they could buy them. Seedsmen emerged, trading hyperadapted local variants like Red Lammas, a strain popular in the 18th century that was known for thriving in chalky soils and making good-quality flour.

Industry observers note that cereals were significant business: The original London Corn Exchange6 was built in 1747; the Paris exchange in 1767; Amsterdam had its own Korenbeurs more than a century earlier. From 1765, Britons began importing wheat with the express purpose of finding better varieties, and middlemen living in other countries would send samples of promising grains to contacts in Britain. Yields reflect the results of an increasingly commercialized sector. After stasis for hundreds of years, then steady 2.5% per decade growth in the previous two centuries, yields grew 60% between 1805 and 1865.

According to recent reports, in the 19th century, progress was still driven by entrepreneurs, usually curious farmers, rather than scientists. One key innovation, pioneered by Patrick Shirreff in Scotland and John Le Couteur in Jersey, was transitioning from selecting a handful of the best plants to breed from, to selecting the best single individual plant, and multiplying it. They didn’t understand the underlying biology, but the results were clear.

In addition to producing more of the best strains, repeated selection and rebreeding of individuals made the traits of the multiplied strains more consistent from generation to generation. As with shattering seed heads 10,000 years earlier, rebreeding meant undesirable genetic variants were eliminated from the population. Early breeders called this “breeding true,” and though the genetic basis for it was not yet understood, it was crucial to farmers, who prefer more consistent and predictable crops.

In a recent development, another crucial development was the intentional crossing of two plants to create a hybrid. A wheat plant can self-pollinate because it contains both male and female reproductive organs, fertilizing its ovules with its own pollen. The overwhelming majority of wheat plants are produced in this way, and therefore have just one parent, which acts genetically as both mother and father. This process doesn’t produce clones initially because each pollen grain or ovule, even from the same individual, is genetically distinct. But it does result in offspring with extremely limited genetic diversity, which diminishes even further with each successive generation of self-breeding.7.

But sometimes cross-pollination produces plants that come from two parents rather than one. In nature this occurs randomly, but plant breeders deliberately take pollen from one plant and use it to fertilize the ovule of another. Shirreff was a pioneer of this technique, too. The best offspring resulting from these crosses would outperform both parents on some key traits. These high-performing varieties would then be multiplied and the seed sold to farmers.

These techniques were adopted throughout Europe, where the Vilmorin Seed Tech giant in France and the Swedish Seed Association in Sweden were among the first to institutionalize cereal breeding. In 1884, The Technology of Bread-Making identified as many as 65 wheat varieties, local and imported, available in English grain markets.

In a recent development, before the Industrial Revolution, Britain was a largely agricultural nation. But by the end of the 19th century, the population had increased more than sevenfold from about 4 million people in 1600 to 30 million in 1900, and only a tenth of workers were employed in agriculture. This would have been impossible without improvements in agricultural yields. The “dark satanic mills” of the Industrial Revolution needed wheat just as much as they needed coal and child labor.

The pace of improvement increased as researchers began to understand more about genetics and evolution. The discoveries of Darwin (natural selection) and Mendel (the inheritance of simple genetic traits, like seed shattering) were essential to understanding why and how techniques applied over the previous centuries had worked. Also critical were contributions of Wilhelm Johannsen, who untangled how much traits were shaped by genes as opposed to the environment, and Ronald Fisher, the “father of modern statistics,” who figured out the underlying maths. Fisher also highlighted how continuous traits like height could be determined by the cumulative effect of many individual genes. These insights, around 100 years ago, led to the development and widespread adoption of statistical tools to identify the best seed varieties and to predict how their offspring would perform.

Breeders generated a vast array of new varieties for testing through a combination of exploration and crossing. Exploration, which was often sponsored by the state, meant collecting seeds from the many unique wheat varieties that had proliferated across the earth since the dawn of time. Britain’s Watkins Landrace Wheat Collection, for example, created in the 1930s, acquired more than 800 wheat cultivars from 32 countries, which could be crossed to create more than 300,000 new hybrid varieties. The USDA had the largest program. Using genetic material from these collections, nurseries would generate crosses for initial testing, multiplying the seeds until there were enough to carry out trials. Trials across several locations allowed researchers to distinguish the effects of genes and environment.

But there were still constraints holding back wheat yields. One was wheat rust, a fungal disease that leaves a characteristic orange-brown powdery residue on plants before shriveling and killing them. Ancient writers knew about this disease: The Romans even had a yearly festival, the Robigalia, in which they performed rituals meant to keep it at bay. In the worst-affected years of the mid-20th century, wheat rust was killing off nearly 20% of American wheat. Breeding programs developed resistant varieties, but any respite was short-lived as the fungus would rapidly evolve a upcoming line of attack.

Another was wheat plants “lodging,” or falling over under their own weight. Fertilizer had become much cheaper thanks to the Haber-Bosch process for making ammonia from nitrogen gas, developed in 1909. But its usefulness for improving wheat production was limited because although fertilizer could in theory make the plants grow larger than before, applying it would often make the stems collapse, making the wheat unharvestable.

At the time, these problems seemed to show that there were fundamental trade-offs limiting yields. It was assumed that further improvements would be incremental. This fueled worry that there would soon be insufficient food for the growing global population; biologist Paul Ehrlich predicted in 1968 that “in the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death.”.

It has been revealed that these gloomy forecasts turned out to be dead wrong. Between 1950 and 1990, wheat yields in many countries — rich and poor — doubled, as did the yields of other crops: the fastest improvement to farming efficiency ever seen. This explosive growth, enabled by advances in breeding together with mechanization and the wider adoption of fertilizer, is referred to as the “Green Revolution.” Norman Borlaug, an American agronomist often called the father of the Green Revolution, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work. In 2009 the director of the World Food Programme said that Borlaug “saved more lives than any man in human history.”.

Sources indicate that borlaug didn’t discover anything new — he just implemented existing techniques better than anyone had before. In 1944, he joined the Mexican Agriculture Program (an initiative founded and funded by the Rockefeller Foundation) under which he produced about 6,000 new crosses over a decade, a huge quantity at a time when most breeders managed fewer than 200 per year. This quantity was essential to generating the high-performing outliers that could become popular new varieties. It is even more notable when two traits you want (like yield and gluten content) are negatively correlated: The more varieties you test, the likelier you are to find one that bucks the trend, performing well on both.

It has been revealed that rather than approaching yield directly, the program focused on two main limiting factors: wheat rust and lodging. The intensive program of crossing and selecting made it possible to develop varieties that carried several forms of resistance to rust at once, and crossbreeding with Japanese “dwarf” wheat varieties, which were shorter and more robust, produced plants that could be juiced up with fertilizer without collapsing. By the 1960s, Borlaug had produced wheat varieties that had it all: resistance to lodging, multiple resistance to wheat rust, and high yields.

One way this breeding program differed from previous ones was that it was split between two separate regions. The original purpose of this was to squeeze two growing seasons into one year, halving the time it took to produce a latest generation. After producing the first generation of offspring in the Toluca highlands, west of Mexico City, Borlaug moved the plants north to the lower-altitude Yaqui Valley, then produced the second generation in time to move back south for the following year. In these stages, selection was crude: Only varieties that failed to germinate or were affected by rust were culled. But later stages of the breeding program included yield trials and statistical selection methods.

Alternating between two regions had another, perhaps serendipitous, benefit.8 By advancing candidates that survived in both locations, Borlaug had selected those that could perform well across different environments. Selection for photoperiod-insensitive seeds (those able to mature in both despite differing daylight exposure) meant that varieties developed in Mexico might be successfully grown in other countries, and therefore could be shared across the world. Not all plants, and certainly not all wheat, can be photoperiod insensitive, but varieties tested by the Mexican Agriculture Program were, which may explain why wheat was the first crop to flourish in the Green Revolution. Maize, for example, is so sensitive that breeders operate semi-independent breeding programs for different latitudes.

Sources indicate that if Ehrlich was aware of this work when he predicted mass starvation in 1968, he cannot have known its significance. In the mid-1960s, India and Pakistan began importing Borlaug’s new wheat varieties. One descendant of these imported wheats (called Kalyan Sona or “golden savior”) performed extremely well and became one of the most commonly planted varieties in the region. From 1965 to 1975, wheat yields in India and Pakistan nearly doubled;9 production increased so much and so quickly that there were shortages of labor for harvest. Over time, other less developed countries followed a similar path.

Industry observers note that the next stage of plant breeding was identifying specific genes for the precise properties that farmers wanted. The problem was that genotyping and genome sequencing were expensive and slow. The first genome was sequenced in 1977, but it belonged to a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) with a genome nearly a million times smaller than a human’s. Sequencing the first human genome cost somewhere between $300 million and $3 billion, and was achieved much later. And this was just a diploid human genome. Wheat has a genome five times larger than that, partly because of its three hybridized subgenomes.

Breeders came up with a comparatively quick and dirty solution: marker-assisted selection. Instead of tracking genes directly, they used much cruder tests to find genetic features (“markers”) that correlated with given traits. One technique was restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis, in which scientists use enzymes to chop DNA into pieces and then literally measure how long the resulting fragments are by how quickly they are pulled through gel by an electric current. While breeders would not know which genes were responsible for traits, they would know that a trait was correlated with a particular pattern of fragment lengths when cut with a particular enzyme.

Sources indicate that despite the crudeness of the method, it still worked for some traits, especially simple ones like rust resistance, which is often controlled by one or two genes. This allowed farmers and breeders to work out whether a variety was going to be good without going through a whole season of growing, as Norman Borlaug had to. This marker-assisted selection for many crops became routine in the 1990s. Field trials remained important, but most strains were filtered out at the marker identification stage, and few ever made it to the field. At the beginning of the decade, only a few hundred markers were known, but by the end, this had expanded to thousands.

Early marker-assisted selection was of limited use for traits like yield, which are influenced by thousands of genes. But we are no longer restricted to looking at a small number of genetic markers. DNA sequencing costs have decreased by a factor of 100,000 since 2000. Now breeders will often use “genomic selection”: essentially, using the entire genome as a marker and letting statistical software predict which genomes are associated with different traits. Genomic selection can tell us if 500 different genes each contribute 0.2% to a trait where traditional marker-assisted selection would have been useless.

Sources indicate that this has revolutionized the process of plant breeding — if not the outcome.10 Global crop yields continue to increase at a steady rate, reflecting the fact that progress is getting harder to come by. We can now use the same genetic prediction tools for complex traits, like yield, grain quality, and drought tolerance, that we once did for simple ones. At the time Norman Borlaug was working, it took months or years and thousands of wheat plants to evaluate a latest variety’s performance. Today, it can take just days to germinate a seedling and make predictions based on a small leaf sample.

Pessimists would say that wheat domesticated us, that we have spent thousands of years in backbreaking labor serving its reproductive ends. Optimists would argue our coevolution has benefited humanity far more, liberating us from a state of subsistence and creating a caloric surplus to sustain the lives of billions.

According to recent reports, the human species used to live hand to mouth: Virtually all our labor was devoted to growing and harvesting food to fend off starvation. Now, in most developed countries, only a tiny fraction of the population works in agriculture. Wheat’s astonishing success is a crucial part of this change. It is the most widely grown crop on earth, covering 1.5% of the planet’s total land area, and is responsible for one-fifth of the world’s calorie intake. But the amount of labor required to produce those calories has decreased enormously. Since 1900, despite the world’s population increasing more than fourfold, the price of wheat is roughly a quarter of what it was.

That transformation is the result of sustained, incremental improvement to yield, to pathogen resistance, to ease of harvest, to taste, to gluten content, and much more. The advancements came from early farmers unknowingly favoring larger seeds; from finicky varieties that couldn’t handle frost, drought, and other hardships being killed off by the elements; and from breeders making active choices about what traits they wanted to cultivate, increasingly backed by the might of modern science. Today, we can sequence wheat’s entire genome and select for exactly the traits we want. Advances in breeding mean that similar stories can be told for every other major crop and farm animal. Each of us now enjoys the fruits of these advances at every mealtime.

In a recent development, A lot has changed since the first wheat was farmed in the Fertile Crescent. But Enki is just as correct now as he was thousands of years ago: We would have no Sumer without grain.

Gemini's New AI Agent Is Surprisingly Useful (If You Use Google for Everything)

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that google loves a rebrand.
  • It has been revealed that to use Task, open Gemini and create a new chat.
  • Of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that google loves a rebrand. What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app. Google took its Spark AI agent, which used to live in a separate tab, and integrated it into the Gemini interface. Gemini Task is available globally, and it’s completely free to use for some. That noted, some features are limited to the U.S. and, of course, subject to some pretty strict usage limits. While not exactly a replacement for ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, you can think of Gemini Task as a controlled version of an AI agent that can do quite a lot in the background.

It has been revealed that to use Task, open Gemini and create a new chat. You’ll see a Task tab next to Chat. Switch to it, and start writing your prompt. (You’ll also see some suggested options here.) Type your task or action and press "Send." The feature works best if you’ve already enabled Personal Intelligence on your Google account, and have connected services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos as well. You can then tag “@Gmail” to use your Gmail account, or even a third-party connector. Task natively supports automation, so you can say something like, "run this task once every day," and the AI will add it to your Scheduled Tasks section.

Of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks. And, in my experience, it works really well. It reminded me of this article's due date, that I have a couple of pitches in my inbox to review, that a credit card bill is due soon, and that there are some holidays around the corner.

Sources indicate that gemini is very good at retrieving information from emails and taking action. For example, I created an automation that collects all my coffee orders for the month and presents the data in Google Sheets. I then asked Task to create a subscription manager for me. Instead of paying for a third-party app, it took a few minutes to collate the services I pay for into one list. It even accounted for the currency differences (some subscriptions are in USD, some in INR) and gave me a tally in INR, along with things like average monthly cost, and more.

In a recent development, while Gemini can connect to the open web, it's quite a hostile place right now for an AI bot. Websites are blocking agents from accessing their pages, which hinders their effectiveness. I asked Gemini to create a task that monitors the price of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones daily. For this, it asked my permission to spin up a remote browser, and loaded up Amazon, only to be blocked instantly. It did succeed in opening Croma though (a national retailer in India), but it took almost a minute for it to figure out that the price had not dropped below what I asked for. Would it be quicker and less resource-intensive if I did this myself? Yes, but the fact that Gemini can do this every evening like clockwork is the real advantage—as long as the websites comply, that is.

If you're going to try Task in Gemini for free, there are some limitations you should know about. The free plan only lets you run tasks once per day, and you can’t be granular about the exact timing. (Paid Gemini plans have no such restrictions.) You can only run 10 tasks at the same time, while the limit is 50 tasks for AI Pro users. Compute-based usage limits will also apply, based on your plan. The free access is right now live in India, the U.S., Canada, Australia, Japan, and South Korea.

Some features, though, are only for U.S. users. Gemini’s feature that lets you call businesses on your behalf is restricted to the States, as is the ability to forward emails to [email protected] to automatically turn the contents of the email into a task (like adding a college schedule to your calendar). U.S. users can also connect their Google Wallet account to set up payments at supported stores.

Gemini Task is not a proactive agent, nor is it trying to be. You still have to check the work. You have to approve any vital steps, and if a website blocks AI models, there’s not a lot Gemini can do about it. For someone like me, who’s all-in on the Google ecosystem, I do see value in Gemini Task. The deep and robust Gmail integration is worth it alone. If you’re on the free plan, set up a couple of background tasks related to Gmail, Google Drive, or background research that run every morning, and call it a day. And if you’re paying for AI Pro, you can get a lot more done.

Offering support for iPhone and Android’s tracking networks, the newly introduced Kodak SlideTag offers the neat added functionality over an AirTag of being able to show your photos and more on an E-Ink display.

Industry observers note that the Kodak SlideTag is inspired by classic 35mm slides from Kodak cameras, and is built by the same company, Reto, that launched a keychain digital camera inspired by old Kodak cameras too. The tracker’s E-Ink display is designed mainly to showcase your photos, with storage built-in for up to 12 photos, but also the ability to show lists and QR codes.

The SlideTag’s extra features are controlled by the Kodak Memory Link app, while tracking is handled in the Find My app on iPhone just like an AirTag (and the Find Hub app on Android phones).

There are nine total styles for the SlideTag, all sold in a blind box format. You can order one tracker for $35 with the whole set also available for purchase.

Eight of the styles have a one-in-eight chance of finding, while the ninth style is only found in one out of every 64 boxes.

Kodak SlideTag is available today from Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iconic YouTube app icon that looked like a retro TV found on iOS might be making a comeback, with newly introduced customizable icons showing up behind the scenes of a new YouTube revision.

In the early days of the iPhone, Apple built a custom app for YouTube on iOS before Google built its own. That included an app icon that looked like a retro TV and it was later replaced when YouTube’s official app debuted on the platform.

Now, that icon might be coming back.

According to recent reports, android Authority spotted several new app icons YouTube for Android is testing in its latest beta update (v21.47.483-BETA). These icons seem to be tied to a new feature that would allow people to customize the homescreen icon for YouTube, and includes seven designs in total including two throwback designs. One is the aforementioned retro TV icon used on iOS, which was never on YouTube for Android, and another is an old stacked YouTube logo design.

That said, it’s very fun to get these throwbacks, and we’ll be excited to see this functionality go live.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Brad Pitt first sued Angelina Jolie in 2022, he accused his ex-wife of unlawfully going behind his back to sell her stake in Château Miraval, the former couple’s prized winery in the south of France.

Jolie responded with a countersuit in October 2022, saying she had done “everything within her control” to make their business partnership work, only to have Pitt seize creative control and overrule her on extravagant projects, allegedly including a fifth swimming pool costing one million euros.

She then raised the stakes considerably, claiming Pitt had turned “physically and emotionally abusive” toward her and their children during an outburst on a private plane in 2016 that led to the collapse of their marriage. Jolie noted she initially considered selling her stake in Miraval to Pitt, realizing it would eventually go to their children, but the deal fell apart when Pitt allegedly demanded a non-disparagement clause she blasted as an “unconscionable gag order.”.

On Wednesday, the former Hollywood power couple declared they reached a private settlement in their nearly five-year legal war, heading off a public and potentially bruising trial set for next August.

“We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further,” Pitt and Jolie said in a joint statement issued by their representatives. “Any comments in media stories attributed to ‘sources’ are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us.”.

In a recent development, as of Wednesday afternoon, no request for dismissal appeared on the court docket. A review of the previously contentious case remained scheduled for Dec. 7.

Latest Update: How did pinwheel calculators work?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as a handful of readers might know, I am a bit of a calculator nerd.
  • A video is worth a thousand tokens, so to explore the ingenuity of these designs, let’s start with a short clip of a Vaucanson calculator from my collection:.
  • In the first half of the video, I demonstrate addition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as a handful of readers might know, I am a bit of a calculator nerd. I’m especially fond of mechanical four-function calculators that had their heyday between the 1920s and 1960s and then disappeared without a trace.

A video is worth a thousand tokens, so to explore the ingenuity of these designs, let’s start with a short clip of a Vaucanson calculator from my collection:.

In the first half of the video, I demonstrate addition. I calculate 1234 + 4321 by placing the first operand in the input register (top), turning the crank clockwise to add this value to the accumulator (bottom right), and then entering the second operand and cranking again. To subtract from the stored value, I’d instead turn the crank counterclockwise.

It has been revealed that the second and more interesting half shows multiplication: I solve 79 × 123 by entering the first operand and then turning the crank three times to load 79 × 3 into the accumulator. Next, I shift the accumulator carriage one decimal digit to the right and crank twice; because the accumulator is offset from the input register, this has the same effect as cranking twenty times in the original position; in other words, I add 79 × 20. Finally, I shift the carriage once more and complete one more turn to add 79 × 100. Note that the crank counter in the bottom left now reads “123”, confirming that we multiplied the first operand by the correct value.

To divide, I’d load the first operand into the accumulator and then successively subtract power-of-ten multiples of the second number. This would give me the integer result in the counter register and the remainder in the accumulator.

Industry observers note that alright — so how does this work? Well, if you pop open a pinwheel calculator, you will be greeted by a pretty complicated mechanism:.

There’s a lot going on here, but the most vital part of the assembly is the cylindrical stack of input disks, one per digit, as seen in the top right of the photo. Each disk has three main components: a center section mounted to a keyed shaft that stays in position until the main crank is turned; a set of nine radial pins that slide into grooves in that disk; and a freely-moving digit-setting ring with a track and a couple of detent positions:.

It has been revealed that each pin has a protrusion that rides in the track of the digit-setting ring. By turning the input lever one way or the other, we can change the number of pins that extend from the assembly.

When the crank is turned, the entire assembly rotates and these extended pins mesh to an intermediate gear that advances the digit at the corresponding position of the accumulator:.

Of course, this mechanism is not enough: without a way to carry to the next column, 0001 + 0009 would give us 0000 instead of 0010. To implement carry, each input disk (except for the rightmost one) is also equipped with a spring-loaded carry pin. This pin sticks out at all times, but is normally out of the path of the intermediate gear — offset to the right — so it has no effect on the output value.

To actually perform carry, each digit of the accumulator is equipped with a cam that shoves a wedge-shaped carry-sensing lever into the path of the carry pin just as the value rolls over from 9 to 0. This wedge in turn deflects the carry pin to the left, momentarily placing it in the path of the intermediate gear for the next decimal digit.

This is a mouthful; the entire process is shown in the following video:.

The carry-sensing lever is pushed back into the home position before the drum completes a full rotation, thus resetting the mechanism.

Note that the carry pins are staggered and do not engage at all once; this is to allow carry to effortlessly ripple through all digits if necessary (e.g., when adding 9999 + 1).

In a recent development, there’s a couple of additional convenience and reliability features in each pinwheel calculator; this includes interlocks to prevent out-of-sequence inputs, as well as reset levers for each register. There’s even a mechanical bell on overflow or underflow. I won’t bore you with all the gory details, in part because these mechanisms are less interesting — but if you’re morbidly curious, this ancient YouTube video provides a more complete walkthrough.

And if you want to learn about the prehistory of calculators, I invite you to check out my 2023 article:.

Recent findings suggest that PS. Yep, this is why one of the registers on all Intel CPUs, used as the implicit destination for some opcodes, is called the “accumulator”.

  • Recent findings suggest that 9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off.
  • According to recent reports, one of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone consumers when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently revealed four upcoming features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now.

Recent findings suggest that 9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

According to recent reports, one of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface. The new interface makes it much easier to switch between different cards during the checkout flow on websites and in apps.

In the new design, you can easily swipe between cards on the main Apple Pay checkout screen. You can also tap on a card to view a grid of all your available Apple Pay cards.

The design also makes it easier to see information about individual cards, including rewards, balances, pay later options, and more.

In a recent development, iOS 27 was released to everyone last week. You can enhancement in the Settings app on your iPhone.

Apple and American Express recently announced a new partnership that lets you pay with American Express rewards points.

When shopping online or in apps with an American Express card, you’ll see a fresh “Use Rewards” option alongside your available Membership Rewards points balance. You can apply points to cover all or part of your purchase, right in the Apple Pay checkout flow.

Recent findings suggest that american Express points redeemed via Apple Pay are valued at 0.7 cents each. For example, this means 10,000 points can be redeemed for $70 applied towards your purchase.

In iOS 27, Apple is adding a newly introduced “Tap to Share” feature that integrates with Apple Pay on iPhone for in-store shopping.

Recent findings suggest that this feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:.

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

iPhone customers with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

This one isn’t really a new feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has announced that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.

As of November, Walmart’s roll out of Apple Pay across the United States is complete.

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

Recent findings suggest that how often do you use Apple Pay? What are your favorite Apple Pay features? Let us know down in the comments.
