Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3495 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen highlights my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

Sources indicate that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

In a recent development, yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Recent findings suggest that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

Recent findings suggest that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Industry observers note that remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga indicates. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Latest York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

It has been revealed that in the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics manufacturer XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” claims Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Sources indicate that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

According to recent reports, after preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

According to recent reports, absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga indicates.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more notable than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell indicates. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” indicates neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

In a recent development, medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, indicates experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” indicates neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Sources indicate that telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra notes, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

It has been revealed that “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

Sources indicate that in the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell indicates. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

Recent findings suggest that the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as rapidly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell states. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

Industry observers note that A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

In a recent development, sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga notes they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this upcoming technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print glitch as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coros has unveiled the Vertix 4, an “expedition-focused” revision to the Vertix 2 and 2S. Coros says it pairs the brand's brightest display yet with long battery life, and after unboxing it myself, I can definitely say it has a more refined feel that could indeed suit the office as well as the summit.

This watch is being marketed as a major step up from the Vertix 2S, with an AMOLED display, a more refined design, satellite maps and, for the first time on a Coros watch, a built-in flashlight. The Vertix 4 will be available to buy starting on Black Friday, Nov. 27, but it won't exactly be at a discount: It costs $799, a $100 increase over the Vertix 2S.

That price does still undercut the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, which starts at $999, though some rivals are cheaper still. For instance, the Suunto Vertical 2 steel model costs $599, and the Garmin Fenix 8 is at the moment on sale for $749.99 at Amazon.

I've only just started testing the Vertix 4 and haven't even had enough time to get through its substantial battery life, but I can share some first impressions, particularly in how it compares with the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro that debuted earlier this year.

Sources indicate that built-in flashlights have become a must-have feature on premium sports watches, and now the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get one. Coros has departed from the usual layout, though. Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit put the light on top of the watch, but Coros places it on the side, between the digital dial and the back button.

Previous Vertix watches used a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display. MIP has advantages, most notably longer battery life, but I know I much prefer the vibrant display on AMOLED screens, like on the Vertix 4. It is the biggest visual change and a large part of why the watch looks more premium than its predecessors.

Recent findings suggest that coros claims up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on. It also quotes 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on. I haven't had time to test these claims properly, so stay tuned.

Coros watches are high-quality sports watches, but don't expect to find all the little lifestyle features you've come to expect on a more traditional smartwatch:.

It has been revealed that music: It can store tracks, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch. It doesn't pair with streaming services.

Payments: There is no NFC payment support.

Watch faces: Customization is more limited than on rivals.

Sources indicate that on paper, the Vertix 4 looks like a significant upgrade: a better display, a more attractive design, a flashlight and satellite maps, at a price well below the Fenix 9 line-up. The $100 increase and cheaper alternatives like the Suunto Vertical 2 and discounted Fenix 8 will matter to some buyers, as will the limited smart features.

  • This shift changes how devices are designed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

Industry observers note that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Recent findings suggest that if you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. In a recent development, if you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, presently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. Bono Bowl Review: U2 Delivers Halftime Goods & Hits On Netflix & NFL’s First Thanksgiving Eve Game, With A Little Help From Dolly Parton

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1201 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deadline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • No matter how many hits and tricks U2 pulled out of the hat at L.A.’s SoFi Stadium, today’s Bono Bowl on Netflix was always going to live in the shadow of the streamer’s square dancing filled Beyoncé Bowl from Christmas Day 2024.
  • Accepting the inevitable, the elder statesmen of anthem rock took their halftime spin on stage at the NFL’s first ever Thanksgiving Eve game to go full bread and circuses.
  • All U2 had to do tonight was show everyone they still have gas in the tank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No matter how many hits and tricks U2 pulled out of the hat at L.A.’s SoFi Stadium, today’s Bono Bowl on Netflix was always going to live in the shadow of the streamer’s square dancing filled Beyoncé Bowl from Christmas Day 2024.

Accepting the inevitable, the elder statesmen of anthem rock took their halftime spin on stage at the NFL’s first ever Thanksgiving Eve game to go full bread and circuses. Giving the people and the streamer what they wanted, the nine-minute show wasn’t as dramatic as the presently 13-13 match-up between the hometown L.A. Rams and the Green Bay Packers, but it didn’t have to be.

All U2 had to do tonight was show everyone they still have gas in the tank.

Under those criteria, in their first time headlining on Netflix, the Irish rockers succeeded.

Veering towards the tried and true, Bono, guitarist The Edge, bassiest Adam Clayton and drummer Larry Mullen Jr thundered through their Boomer classics of “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” The Joshua Tree’s “Where The Streets Have No Name” and MLK tribute “Pride (In The Name of Love).” Add to that a sprinkle of The Supremes “Stop! In the Name of Love” via some glorious vocals thrown in from teh Grammy nominated Womack Sisters and the beats of an on-field marching band and you have an All-American party — which is precisely what a NFL halftime show is supposed to be.

Recent findings suggest that U2 performs 'Where The Streets Have No Name' at the NFL Thanksgiving Eve halftime show. pic.twitter.com/dXhj4KQbPk.

In a nod to their latest release and the times we live in, the second song in the set poignantly was the “Torn” duet with Dolly Parton.

Dolly Forever <3 U2 pays tribute to Dolly Parton with “Torn” during their halftime performance pic.twitter.com/c4CfeoQiXi.

With the obvious exception of the inclusion of the late great Dolly, who was displayed on flowing curtains that came down from the stadium roof, it was a set that could have come almost anytime the last 40 years. In fact, besides “Torn” (Parton’s last recording), every song in U2’s Thanksgiving Eve set came from when Ronald Reagan was President.

Bono’s vow not to use backing tracks and the pre-halftime shot that Netflix demonstrated of U2 heading through Sofi’s catacombs on gold carts sorta told you all you needed to know.

Sources indicate that to their credit, unlike most Super Bowl halftime indicates of the past dozen years, (and expected for Jay-Z’s Super Bowl LXI set on February 14 at Sofi), a relatively stripped down U2 didn’t bring on any super star guests for the L.A. crowd. Walking out on the field to a chorus, the usually-chatty band took the in-the-round stage with a “thank you for having us” and said little more.

Oddly ending a bit too promptly, tonight’s shindig came halfway through the NFL’s first Thanksgiving Eve match with the Rams battling it out with Packers at the L.A. team’s camera-ready stadium. A clear belt notch in the league’s desire to dramatically expand the incredibly lucrative football franchise, tonight’s much-hyped game between the Packers and the Rams was given all the gloss of a playoff clash or the Super Bowl itself by the Ted Sarandos and Greg Peter-run streamer.

Having already played a few warm-up gigs — like opening the November 14 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame ceremony — during the extensive promotional tour this month for their recently released Carnaval De Luz album, tonight gave U2 a further chance to reach fans old and fresh. Aided by a stage that was rolled out and set up in less than 8 minutes, a 52-foot telescopic camera crane and a specialty camera coming down from the Sofi roof, the Jesse Collins Entertainment-produced set had a very professional shine.

WHAT A PERFORMANCEU2 performs '(Pride) In The Name of Love' with The Womack Sisters at the NFL Thanksgiving Eve Halftime Show pic.twitter.com/ZBzEZ1SUIt.

Industry observers note that for a soaring-gesture band never shy of taking big stages in a big way, the global reach can only help U2 hawk a few more tickets for their upcoming Greatest Show on Earth tour. The tour begins in Mexico City in February. After indicates in South America and Europe, the band and their unofficial 50th anniversary tour ends up in North America for a 15-stadium run starting in Miami on August 13.

It has been revealed that at the same time, as the Rolling Stones, Bruce Springsteen and many other stadium-playing legacy acts will tell you, the role of old bands is to play the old hits — no matter how good or bad the latest album is. Bono, the Edge, Mullen and Clayton knew that back in 2002 when they played Super Bowl XXXVI in the aftermath of the 9/11 terror attacks. Using their Elevation Tour set at NOLA’s Superdome, U2 in less than 20-minutes whipped off “Beautiful Day,” “MLK” and “Where The Streets Have No Name” and paid tribute via curtain with the names of the fallen on it to those who lost their lives that horrible day in NYC.

One of the biggest bands in the world for 40 years, U2 haven’t toured since 2019, and they had a bit to prove tonight, as they made clear.

Yet, the GameDay halftime show wasn’t their first time on stage this decade.

A 40-show stint at Vegas’ Sphere starting in September 2023 saw the band pulling it off Zoo TV style, even with an injured Mullen sitting it out. Still, a big live draw since the mid-1980s no matter how their records charted, the Irving and Jeffrey Azoff-managed U2 are leaving no opportunity unexplored this year in a hope to return to relevance.

Even Sofi itself got in on the act on Wednesday.

It has been revealed that we are excited to welcome @U2 for their premiere appearance at SoFi Stadium during today's halftime show 🏈 And even more excited for their return on October 1 & 2! Tickets on sale on December 4 on Ticketmaster 🎟️ pic.twitter.com/KnB9CkgIQp.

It has been revealed that with ads galore and L.A. beauty shots tonight, Netflix has finally worked out most of the kinks that marred some of their past live sports events. Fueled by play-by-play from Noah Eagle and analysis from Hall-of-Famer Luke Kuechly, the primetime result so far delivered a slick and seamless product that moved at the pace of the action on the field. Simply put (and hear me Jeff Bezos), Netflix equaled what ESPN and Monday Night Football have been doing for ages — which is no small feat when you consider that the streamer’s initial live sporting event was just over three years ago with the mash-up golf tournament The Netflix Cup.

Industry observers note that from the substantial picture perspective, tonight’s game and that halftime show can’t but help Netflix’s ongoing bid to FIFA for the 2030 World Cup. For U2, the ride may be vintage, but turns out there’s still quite a bit of gas in the old tank.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”.
  • Sources indicate that upgrade 11/24: This new setting is now widely rolling out.
  • Industry observers note that under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the new “Chat content including text & attachments” setting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”.

Sources indicate that upgrade 11/24: This new setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Industry observers note that under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the new “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16: Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”.

Google is now separating that preference into two new options.

According to recent reports, this is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI owners on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:.

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its customers, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”.

The duration is presently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”.

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is at the moment off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

I covered Black Friday sales for years, and these days I spend a lot of my time in the lab at Tom's Guide testing the very same TVs that end up in these sales. That combination has made me picky, but has also given me great deal-finding instincts.

If you only have a moment, here are my two favorite Black Friday TV deals I've seen so far. As the long wait for Grand Theft Auto VI finally ends, South Park‘s celebration was cut short on this week’s episode.

In the finale “City Endings,” outages hit the town (currently rebranded as South America for Season 29) thanks to the AI data centers of Billionaire Weenietown that moved into Butters’ backyard after Mayor McDaniels cut a deal to bring them to town.

A mob visits the mayor, who instead of taking responsibility, leads them to believe the outages are “definitely cyber attacks by the Chinese.” That prompts the mob to stake out Mr. Kim’s City Parlor, where they each end up getting a massage with a “city ending.” Watch on Deadline.

Meanwhile, Kyle, Stan and Cartman are visited by the ghost of Kenny, who previously died when a bomb strapped to his e-bike exploded.

Industry observers note that the trio gives Butters a visit after remembering his connectivity complications while trying to watch Dr. Pimple Popper videos. It turns out, Butters is no longer affected by the outages as he’s since been getting some kickbacks from Billionaire Weenietown, including a massive GTA VI setup.

In the middle of Butters’ gameplay, zombie Kenny appears on the screen, breaking out like Samara in The Ring to deliver a message to his friends.

The episode culminates with the kids confronting the cops and the mayor, only to find out they were all complicit in Kenny’s death when they allowed the billionaires to come to South Park.

Ultimately, Mayor McDaniels takes responsibility for the billionaires ruining the town but sends Mr. Kim to space on WeenieX in order to appease the town. The show ends with “America” falling off the South Park sign after they rolled over to change the town’s name for Trump.

South Park‘s finale wrapped up its Billionaire Weenietown storyline with some more topical jabs, following the massively unprecedented release of GTA VI, as well as the ongoing nationwide outages, which the government has chalked up to many networks changing over to AI systems.

The U8QG also has plenty to offer gamers using a current-generation console or a capable gaming PC. It supports refresh rates up to 165Hz, variable refresh rate, and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, with a measured 4.3 milliseconds of input lag at 1080p and 120Hz and 10.1 milliseconds at 4K and 60Hz. Those results should make controls feel responsive, even during fast-paced games. There’s also a side-mounted USB-C port that accepts DisplayPort video, while Google TV handles streaming alongside Apple AirPlay and Google Cast. The biggest inconvenience is the limited selection of three HDMI ports, since a console, soundbar, and streaming device would occupy all of them.

What does the "best mattress deals" mean?

Before I delve into each of the best Black Friday mattress deals, I want to start by clarifying what I mean by the "best mattress deals".

I consider the best mattress deals to A) feature a mattress that was awarded three stars or above by our expert team or online customers and B) meet at least one of the following criteria:.

1. It isn't the usual discount — it's better. For example, a mattress that is usually 20% in the regular monthly mattress sales suddenly dropping to 30% off during the Black Friday period.

Sources indicate that 3. It's the usual discount, but still outstanding value for money. For example, a mattress in a price tier that's beneath its actual performance (such as a luxury mattress regularly sold at a mid-range price).

It has been revealed that at Tom's Guide we use a diverse panel of sleep experts to test the most popular mattresses you can find online. We combine repeatable, scientific lab measurements with extended at-home sleep trials. Their review process is also editorially independent and free from brand influence.

Sources indicate that rather than relying solely on first impressions, we use standardized, objective lab tests to generate reliable, unbiased data. For instance, we use thermal imaging camera tests to see how well a mattress regulates temperature, and use accelerometers to test how well a mattress isolates motion.

Lab numbers do not tell the whole story, so a lead reviewer sleeps on each mattress at home for at least three weeks — the typical time it takes for a person's body to adjust to a upcoming bed. We also gather feedback from a testing panel made up of people with different body types and sleeping positions to account for subjective comfort.

It has been revealed that with a design that looks like the love child of the AirPods Max and the Beats Studio Pro, these have an adjustable telescoping frame and a unique modular design that lets you mix and match ear pad colors. Sources indicate that they’re controlled by two buttons on each earcup and powered by a dedicated Beats chip, with support for both Android devices and iPhones. They last up to 32 hours with ANC on, which is longer than both the more expensive Sony WH-1000XM6 and AirPods Max 2.

Recent findings suggest that according to Beats, the 360 offer up to 1.75 times the noise cancellation of the Beats Studio Pro. PCMag’s review, which gave the headphones an “Excellent” rating, was impressed by how well they blocked out everything from plane engine noise to café chatter. The noise cancellation falls short of pricier models, and PCMag found the Sony WH-1000XM4C slightly better in that respect.

The PCMag review claims the headphones deliver “nice, deep bass, reasonably crisp highs, and a more neutral tuning than you might expect for a pair of Beats headphones.” If you’re after long battery life, rich audio, and plush earcups you can swap for a pop of color, $249 is a great price for the Beats 360 headphones.

iOS 27 brought fresh features to Apple Wallet, Maps, Notes, Messages, and more—and it includes key upgrades for the Mail app too. Here’s everything new for Apple Mail in iOS 27.

If you have much history using Apple Mail, you’ll know that its search feature hasn’t always been the best. But in iOS 27, search has gotten a big upgrade.

More relevant search in Mail. A new ranking system brings the most relevant results to the top to help you find what you need right away — even if it’s buried deep in your inbox.

Sources indicate that I can’t count the number of times search has previously failed to find messages that I knew existed. So far in my usage, iOS 27 has fixed that.

Suggestions at the top of messages have been in Apple Mail for years. But in iOS 27, they have a upcoming, more flexible design and expand to support third-party apps.

When Mail detects that you might want to take action on the contents of an email, a suggestion might appear at the top of the message. These include: directions in Maps, creating events in Calendar, tracking a shipment with Apple Wallet, and more.

In iOS 27, third-party apps can offer suggestions too. And when multiple apps are available with suggested actions, there’s a drop-down menu to show you all available options.

Smart Reply is a keyboard feature that automatically surfaces reply options you can utilize with a single tap.

In iOS 27, the next generation of Apple Intelligence comes with improvements to Smart Reply.

Apple states that Smart Reply “can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.” Essentially, rather than offering fairly generic reply options, now Smart Reply suggestions will actually sound a lot more like you.

Industry observers note that apple has added ‘Ask Siri’ buttons throughout Apple Mail, just like the rest of its system apps. And Siri AI brings a bunch of new powers for Mail customers.

One example I’ve seen several times on social media is that you can ask Siri to delete all messages from a specific sender that’s spamming you.

I asked the new Siri on iOS 27 to delete Spam emails from a particular adddess and it just did that so seamlessly pic.twitter.com/EYn74buYAX.

EXCLUSIVE: Lauren Ash (Superstore) and Mae Martin (Wayward) have been cast in Dirts, an ensemble adult animated high-school comedy series for New Metric Media‘s streaming service Shozer.

They will appear alongside the likes of Ash’s Superstore co-star Mark McKinney, Mark Little (Gary and His Demons) and Ryan Belleville (Workin’ Moms).

The show, set to premiere in winter 2027, follows Gus (Little) and Brus (Belleville), two deeply unpopular vegetable teenagers trying to survive life at Leguma Beach High, where high-society vine vegetables mingle with scrappy root transplants. The unlikely friends have to navigate the indignities of adolescence in a world where school politics can get particularly rotten. Related Stories Casting Lauren Ash, Mae Martin & Randall Park Join Crave Comedy 'Meatballs' News Samantha Bee Sitcom 'The Ambassador' Toplines CBC's Latest Slate.

According to recent reports, ash plays Sproutabella, Martin is Trevin Stems and McKinney Principal Corny. Also in the voice cast are Kyle Dooley (Cupcake & Dino: General Services) as Eggmilio and Butternut; Evany Rosen (Total Dramarama) as Cheryl and Snap Pea; Kayla Lorette (Doomlands) as Pep and Ms. Jicama; Rodrigo Fernandez-Stoll (BlackBerry) as Janitor McKale and Theatre Squash; and Chelsea Clark (Ginny & Georgia) as Gabe.

Dane Clark, Viveno Caldinelli and Mark Montefiore co-created the show, with Caldinelli directing. New Metric Media is the producer in partnership with Little Black Stone Studios. Ariel Yang and Max Wolfond are the producers for New Metric, with Tysen Potter in the same role for Little Black Stone. Production will cater for vertical and horizontal viewing, and you can watch a first-look clip above.

Dirts toplines the latest slate for Shozer, the YouTube comedy channel brand that Shoresy and Letterkenny producer Latest Metric introduced last year.

Also greenlit is The Historical History of Canada, a mockumentary series that takes a twisted and satirical look at the most infamous moments in Canadian history. These will include the mysterious fire that destroyed the Parliament building in 1916 and the Toronto Maple Leafs’ latest Stanley Cup win. Fresh Metric’s Lana Maclin, Alona Metzer and Liv Berkowitz are producing.

Elevator Comedy is a 30-part series of 45-second episodes that will give emerging comedy talent a platform, with performers put in close quarters with the audience. As with Dirts, it’s being produced for vertical and horizontal viewing.

The Eh-List, New Metric’s stand-up comedy strand, is also getting specials from Just For Laughs regular Daniel Tirado, veteran comic Alex Wood and viral sensation Drew Behm.

Shozer debuted last year with a slate of shows and films including Lionsgate’s Running Wilde, Van Wilder: Party Liaison and Zack and Miri Make A Porno, along with Letterkenny‘s first YouTube outing, LetterkennyProblems.

“We’ve spent years building comedy franchises and seeing what happens when audiences connect with great characters and creators,” said Montefiore, CEO of Fresh Metric. “With Shozer, we’re applying that experience to a D2C model where we can discover new talent, invest in original ideas and build audience communities.

It has been revealed that “We want Shozer to become a trusted destination for comedy, where people come to discover their next favourite creator or series. And by developing and owning that IP from the outset, we have the flexibility to grow those properties across multiple platforms, formats and consumer experiences.”.

Recent findings suggest that cheat codes have long been a part of the Grand Theft Auto video game franchise, and the tradition continues with GTA 6. Not only does GTA 6 support cheats, but it also has a menu that lists all of them as well as instructions for unlocking them. However, you cannot fire up the game and start using cheats from the beginning. In fact, it requires quite a bit of work on your part. Here's how to unlock cheat codes in GTA 6, how to see the list of cheats, as well as the 10 best cheat codes in GTA 6.

Industry observers note that gone are the good old days when you could fire up GTA, enable god mode, unlimited ammo, no reload, spawn a jetpack, and run around the entire city destroying things at will. In GTA 6, you'll need to complete the main story to unlock the ability to use cheat codes. On top of that, you'll have to complete challenges of various difficulty levels to access specific cheat codes. Some of these cheats unlock the moment you finish the main story. Others, however, are quite challenging or time-consuming. For instance, unlimited reload requires you to win 25 gold medals at shooting ranges.

Once you complete the main story in GTA 6, just go to in-game settings, and you'll see a new Cheats tab. This lists all 61 cheats and how to unlock them. You'll see the actual button combo for each cheat right after you complete the unlock requirement.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, there are some serious gameplay ramifications to using cheat codes in GTA 6. For starters, you can't save the game once you input even one cheat code. That's why it's best to save before you start using cheats, to avoid losing progress. Using cheat codes will also disable trophies and achievements in GTA 6.

Recent findings suggest that to start using cheat codes in GTA 6, you'll have to get your character to pull up the smartphone by pressing the up arrow on the D-Pad. Then, hold L1+R1, and press the cheat's key combination on the D-Pad.

#119829. Industry News: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
