What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s at the moment receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

Industry observers note that there’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

In a recent development, at the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky rapidly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

In a recent development, to underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

In a recent development, though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the organization’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

Sources indicate that these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

Industry observers note that in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Sources indicate that the misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

According to recent reports, even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

In a recent development, what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print glitch as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SAP’s headquarters building in Walldorf, Germany, with the company logo on its roof.

It has been revealed that an SAP employee allegedly passed confidential material from British AI startup Conduct, an SAP partner, to Berlin rival Qorelo, then joined Qorelo, Bloomberg reported. SAP did not tell Conduct after a whistleblower flagged it in October; SAP claims the parties deny the claims.

An SAP employee allegedly passed confidential material from Conduct, a British AI startup that SAP works with and has invested in, to a rival, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday. SAP did not tell Conduct after a whistleblower flagged the matter in October, people familiar with it told Bloomberg.

The employee allegedly gave a Conduct demo and other documents to Berlin-based Qorelo, which also partners with SAP. After the complaint, SAP banned him from its offices. He joined Qorelo in November, according to Bloomberg.

In a recent development, the whistleblower report claims he added about 800 contacts to Qorelo’s customer database while still at SAP. It claims he also shared a recording of a call between SAP, Conduct and their customer DHL.

Conduct learned of the matter this month from a whistleblower, and its lawyers then contacted SAP.

“In this case, we contacted the relevant parties, and they have denied the allegations,” SAP said in a statement.

Qorelo said it takes the claims very seriously and is reviewing the employee’s move from SAP. Conduct declined to comment, and the former employee did not respond.

In a recent development, conduct was founded in 2024 by three former Palantir staff. It raised $60M this year with SAP among the investors, and helps companies move off older SAP systems, a market Qorelo also serves.

In a recent development, the claims could strain the startup ties SAP is using to rebuild around AI. The manufacturer has also frozen most hiring to free up cash for that push.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As with many home workers, I’m very lucky to have a dedicated office space that doubles as a PC gaming space when the working day is done, but as the nights draw closer and it gets much darker sooner (at least here in the UK), I’ve been looking for alternative options to keeping my room lighting on to avoid overpowering my eyes.

According to recent reports, enter BenQ, with the manufacturer offering its ScreenBar® Max to check out. With it, I’ve gone from being desperate to get out of the office before it gets dark to never wanting to leave.

I’ve used multiple screen-mounted lighting options in the past, but it would be fair to say the ScreenBar Max goes further than many of its contemporaries.

I work nine-hour days and often hop back on in the evenings to get additional projects finished, and that means I’ve been looking for something to help me do my best work regardless of time of day.

Industry observers note that the trouble is that many of these light bars illuminate one spot on a desk, focusing on a relatively small section of the workspace. That’s particularly troublesome in my use case because I have a dual-monitor setup, meaning there’s more surface area to cover, and they’ve just not been up to the task - until now.

BenQ’s ScreenBar Max is wide enough to allow for minimal glare since it’s not centred on a specific spot, and has done a great job of keeping me focused and locked in well into the evenings.

In a recent development, this is achieved with what BenQ calls its ASYM-TriZone Light and a 36-degree shielding angle, which prevents the light from pointing directly at the user. This means the light stays where you want it to be (across your desk) and not in your peepers.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With up to 700 lux of brightness and a colour temperature that moves from 2700K to 6000K, it’ll automatically adjust to find the ANSI-recommended 1:3 contrast ratio.

Sources indicate that I’m also pleased to say that backlighting on offer is very welcome. Too often, working on a desk with a light bar can feel a little like working in a cave, and this helps illuminate the space behind your desk. It’s a small touch, but it’s very welcome.

My favourite feature of the BenQ ScreenBar Max might be that it slides out handily from the stand to cover more of the desk.

It has been revealed that this means if you have a compatible webcam that allows for desk view, and you’re demonstrating something on your desktop, you can ensure it’s well-illuminated. As someone who plays trading card games with friends online, it’s nice to be able to ensure my playspace is the most reliably lit of anyone in the match.

The ScreenBar Max can achieve this because, rather than putting extra weight on the top of your desk, it sits behind—either on a desk clamp or a dedicated stand—meaning it’s not tied to your monitor setup in the way traditional light bars can be.

Sources indicate that and, while other options have you fussing with buttons and dials to get them activated, the BenQ ScreenBar Max uses the same sensors that BenQ tells me are found in autonomous systems. This means I can walk into the office with my morning coffee, and “voila!” - the lighting activates, automatically adjusted to my space.

As I mentioned earlier, the ScreenBar Max has me dreading those cold winter months less than I was, and I’m almost excited to do my work in a space so well lit for the first time in a long time.

The BenQ ScreenBar Max is available now for £239 from BenQ online and selected retailers.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Messages API is how customers and Anthropic’s own apps, such as Claude Code, reach Claude.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that anthropic has moved its Messages API from Python to Rust with Claude agents writing and fixing much of the code. Its tests could not be trusted, so it compared the two versions on live traffic, and says the newly introduced API uses about 70% less CPU per request.

According to recent reports, anthropic has moved the main API behind Claude from Python to Rust, with Claude agents doing much of the work, the manufacturer said on Wednesday. It switched public traffic over in September without taking offline a service that has suffered outages this year.

The Messages API is how customers and Anthropic’s own apps, such as Claude Code, reach Claude. Anthropic added message threads to it this month to cut delays in long agent sessions.

Anthropic says the API’s traffic grew about 1,800-fold from early 2024 to this autumn. Over that time, it has signed huge compute deals, including with Google and Broadcom. Python, meanwhile, was adding overhead at every step.

Claude wrote a first version of the core code in about a week. Checking it took months. The fresh code passed about 98% of its tests in April, but only about a quarter of real requests matched the old system.

Sources indicate that part of the problem was the tests themselves. Claude had helped port them, and an audit found more than 100 checks that had been weakened.

So Anthropic used live traffic as the test. It ran requests through both versions and compared each step, without reading customers’ text. Claude agents then fixed each difference, with engineers reviewing every fix.

Engineers still had to catch shortcuts. In one case, an agent made the outputs match by copying a missing tool description into files, which an engineer rejected as throwaway code.

In a recent development, the latest API uses about 70% less computing power per request and over 80% less memory, Anthropic indicates. The median wait for the first part of a reply fell about 20% for Claude Code users.

According to recent reports, anthropic has mentioned Claude now writes more than 80% of the code it merges. The tech giant argues that checking AI-written code, not writing it, is now the bottleneck.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re picking between the two lawn mowers, your choice largely depends on the size of the area you’re mowing. For larger properties, the LUBA 3 AWD 3000 is a solid fit. It can also handle slopes as steep as 80%, and its 15.7-inch cutting width and two cutting discs can handle up to 5,400 square feet per hour. The AI vision system allows it to recognise and avoid 300 different types of obstacles, including toys and pets.

Both mowers are designed to remove much of the manual work associated with yard maintenance. Once configured, these mowers can manage multiple mowing zones, customize schedules, and varied cutting heights.

Priced at $1,599, the LUBA mini 2 is a fairly substantial investment, but the $400 Black Friday discount and free wash stand make it a bit easier to justify. If you’ve been considering a robotic lawn mower to bring some automation to the outdoors, these Black Friday offers are worth a look.

According to recent reports, demand for help with AI at work is growing. London’s Multiverse raised $70M in May to sell AI training across Europe. Significant employers are still working it out: Meta planned to cut some teams by up to 60% and hand their work to AI, then cancelled a second round of cuts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring upcoming challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also reveals how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a collection of preserved UI style guides a.k.a. interface guidelines from various companies, starting from the early 1980s and continuing to today.

(Commodore) Amiga was a multimedia personal computer particularly popular in the 1980s and 1990s in Europe. Its GUI was called Workbench.

Android is a mobile operating system and a rival to iOS. The first style guide I could locate was in 2012.

BlackBerry was a beleagured maker of mobile handsets.

Common Desktop Environment (CDE) is a desktop environment for Unix machines, using (and eventually merging with) OSF/Motif widgets.

Common User Access (CUA) is a late 1980s standard for user interfaces that influenced Windows and OS/2.

In a recent development, graphics Environment Manager (GEM) is a 1980s operating system/GUI. It was well-known by customers of the Atari ST computers, known in these circles as TOS.

Sources indicate that GNOME is a desktop environment for Linux and BSD operating systems. Note that the versioning number of these guidelines is very confusing.

iOS (previously iPhone OS) is Appleâs mobile operating system for iPhone smartphones and their siblings.

Java is a programming language, which comes equipped with JFC (Java Foundation Classes) and Swing GUI components.

These are some historical Apple GUI style guides, starting with Lisa in the 1980, and continuing to the âclassicâ Mac OS, with a brief stop in the Apple II corner.

More modern Apple Mac style guides, covering Mac OS X/Aqua and beyond.

An abandoned mobile operating system designed by General Magic.

Guidelines specific to Microsoft Office, in particular covering the use of its ribbon.

It has been revealed that neXTSTEP was NeXTâs influential operating system and graphical user interface. It eventually morphed into OpenStep on one side, and modern Mac OS X on another.

Apple Newton was Appleâs PDA rolled out in 1993 and abandoned in 1998.

Nokia released various style guides for its early smartphones, including its Symbian operating system.

OPEN LOOK is a UNIX graphical user interface, started by Sun and AT&T.

Sources indicate that palm OS was the original graphical operating system for Palmâs mobile devices. Eventually, the organization moved toward webOS, covered elsewhere on this page.

PenPoint was an early tablet operating system developed by GO Corporation for its unsuccessful line of devices.

RISC OS is a British operating system and GUI, developed originally for Acorn computers, and continuing as a community project.

Industry observers note that style guides for various UNIX-based operating system from SGI, or Silicon Graphics Inc. Just like CDE above, these too use the Motif widgets.

Taligent was a troubled software organization, incorporated as an Apple/IBM partnership. One of its fruits was a CommonPoint application framework.

It has been revealed that webOS was a successor to Palm OS that was eventually purchased by HP and later LG Electronics. Today, it is used on smart TVs, refrigerators, and projectors.

Does Microsoft Windows need an introduction? Note a little hole here around 1990, where Microsoft was preoccupied with CUA framework in partnership with IBM.

Style guides for failed mobile Windows efforts, starting with Windows Mobile 6, and continuing through Windows Phone 7.

Thatâs it! Please let me know if you have any thoughts and particularly if you have some style guides that are missing from the above list.

Some of the above mirrors were lightly cleaned up to make their consumption easier â stuff like pixellating images better, inlining images instead of linking to them, or fixing YouTube embeds.

You can also download all the above style guides in one archive.
